A QUASI-2-D MODEL FOR THE PREDICTION OF
THE WALL TEMPERATURE OF ROCKET ENGINE
COOLING CHANNELS

M. Pizzarelli, S. Carapellese, and Francesco Nasuti
Dipartimento di Ingegneria Meccanica e Aerospaziale, Sapienza University of
Rome, Rome, Italy

A simplified quasi-2-D model is developed to study the coupled problem of coolant flow and
wall structure heat transfer in the cooling channels of an liquid rocket engine thrust chambers. This model is based on one-dimensional governing equations for coolant mass conservation and momentum balance, and on a two-dimensional governing equation for coolant
energy balance. The energy balance equation is coupled to the wall heat transfer balance
in the radial direction. The turbulent thermal conductivity, fluid skin friction, and
coolant-wall heat transfer coefficients are evaluated by semiempirical relationships provided
in the literature. This model, which is suited to high aspect ratio cooling channels, permits
fast prediction of both the coolant flow evolution and the temperature distribution along the
whole cooling channel structure. Validation of the model is first carried out by comparison
with straight channel solutions obtained with an experimentally validated CFD solver.
Then, further validation is carried out by using the quasi-2-D model for the analysis of a
regeneratively cooled rocket engine thrust chamber. Results show good agreement with
available data of maximum wall temperature and coolant pressure drop.

1. INTRODUCTION

The design and realization of a liquid rocket engine thrust chamber requires a
thorough analysis to predict wall temperatures, raised by the large heat flux coming
from the combustion gases, and thus to ensure its structural integrity. The need for
thermal analysis is especially important in reusable engines, where an effective and
efficient cooling system is crucial to extend the engine life, or in expander cycle
engines, where coolant warming provides the available power for turbo-machinery.
In these cases, regenerative cooling is usually considered, where one of the propellants, typically the fuel (liquid hydrogen, RP1, liquid methane, etc.), is forced
through passages that are machined inside the thrust chamber wall, then, the heated
fuel is injected into the chamber or goes to turbine. A regenerative cooling technique
provides: no energy loss (thermal energy is absorbed by the coolant and returned to
the injector); no change in wall contour as a function of time; indefinite firing duration; and relatively lightweight construction [1]. However, it has to be kept in mind

that it permits only limited throttling with most coolants, has reduced reliability
with some coolants (e.g., hydrazine), and requires increased pump power because of
the large pressure drop at high heat-flux levels [1]. The trade-off among these aspects
makes regenerative cooling interesting for large high-pressure, high heat-flux thrust
chambers and for expander (and expander-bleed) cycle engines. Thermal analysis of
regeneratively cooled engines is therefore essential to predict not only wall temperature but also coolant temperature and pressure at the channel exit. Moreover, thermal
analysis becomes particularly important if the goal is to search for optimum cooling
channel configuration. An example of such modifications is that of high-aspect-ratio
cooling-channels (HARCC) [2]. In fact, an increase of the channel aspect ratio,
k ¼ h=b, leads to a reduction of the wall temperature on the hot-gas side,
mainly because of the increase of the coolant side surface area (relative to the hot-gas
side surface) by the use of extended surfaces, or ribs (Figure 1). Theoretical and
experimental studies on a high aspect ratio cooling channel for rocket engines have
been conducted by NASA since the 1990s [2–4] to increase the life of the Space Shuttle
main engine. The technological solution of HARCC has also been considered in Europe, where the thrust chamber of the cryogenic engines Vulcain and Vulcain 2
are characterized by cooling passages, with an aspect ratio as high as 8 in the throat
region [5,6].

To design more efficient thrust chambers, cooling channel configurations
should be studied by optimization methods which will include suitable models for

thermal analysis. Unfortunately, a comprehensive thermal model aiming to estimate
wall temperature and coolant pressure drop is rather complex, because it must
account for different phenomena coupled with each other: convection from hot-gas
to the wall, conduction within the wall, and convection form the wall to the cold
fluid. A further complication is that the coolant is often a supercritical fluid, and
methods based on the assumption of perfect gas or incompressible fluid cannot be
used [7]. Finally, it has to be considered that the optimization process consists of
many calculation loops which include thermal and fluid analysis of the coolant flow
in cooling channels, as well as the thermal analysis of the wall structure. As a consequence, the solution of the 3-D Navier Stokes equations coupled with the wall thermal analysis, which would be necessary to describe the regenerative cooling system,
is not suitable. In fact, its computational cost is too high to be part of an optimization process or to understand the role of the main parameters that affect the cooling
system. For this reason one-dimensional models for both coolant and hot-gas flows,
and heavily relying on empirical relationships, are widely used to analyze the regeneratively cooled thrust chambers [4,5,8–12]. Recently, to overcome the simplification
arising from one-dimensional modeling of hot-gas expansion, which fails in the case
of the nozzle with a large expansion rate (e.g., bell-shaped nozzles), efforts have been
